That was the first half. We covered how we ask one question many ways, and what happens when the model writes its reasoning first. Before you go, one question. Which method so far would you try first on your own task? [Wait for answers. Take two.] Good. Think about your choice during the break.

After the break, Part C starts. It's about agents and the harness. That's the loop around the model, how to measure an agent, and how to keep it safe. We continue in ten minutes. I'm here if you have questions.

Part C.html: Welcome back, everyone. Before the break, the model made one call and gave one answer. We only changed its input. Now, in Part C, Prompt as System, the model runs in a loop. It acts, reads the result, and acts again. We'll look at what agents can do today, what an agent is, harness or training, why an agent is a whole system, and how we measure and secure one.

Why prompting · NeurIPS 2026 labs.html: Here's a chart that shows how much of the field is moving to agents. [Point at the poster.] Jueun Kim made it from the official program of NeurIPS 2026. For each lab, it shows the research area that the lab publishes on most, and it compares that with the whole conference. The number 3.7 times means this. Twenty-three percent of Microsoft's papers are on LLM agents, against six percent across the conference. Four of the sixteen labs have agents as their top area. They are Microsoft, Amazon, CMU and Google. Across the conference, the number of LLM-agent papers went from 149 to 357 this year, up 140 percent, while the conference grew 6 percent. So a lot of the work is moving to agents. And what does an agent do all day? It writes. Next, a figure about how much.

Anthropic · Reading Claude as a full-tim.html: Before we ask what agents can do, look at how much they write. [Point at the figure.] This figure comes from Anthropic's own report on how work changes inside the company. It shows the hours per week that one person would need to read all the output of their interactive Claude sessions. The report converts output tokens to words, at zero point seven five words per token, and it assumes two hundred fifty words read per minute. For engineering and research, that's four hundred twenty-four hours a week. For finance it's forty-three hours, for sales thirty-five, and for legal, policy and trust, twenty-six. So how much a model writes is not a small matter. Steering the length of what a model generates takes skill. How much it writes, and when it stops. Keep this in mind in Part C. Now, how capable are agents today?

Anthropic · Agents come to the communica.html: Agents don't only write a lot. They also join the conversation. [The animation starts by itself, runs 15 seconds and loops.] The same Anthropic report looks at Slack, the chat tool where the company talks. The figure shows the network of one large department. Blue dots are employees. Orange dots are agent threads, and a line joins everyone who wrote in the same thread. At the start there are a hundred and fifty-five employees and a hundred and fifty agent threads. At the end there are two hundred and thirty-seven employees and seven thousand nine hundred and twenty-two agent threads, and the orange dots dominate. The report says that agents spread through Slack and eventually appeared in nearly half of active, public channels. If the video doesn't play, read the title and the legend. Now, how capable are agents today?

CMU 2 · Agents wrote a C compiler.html: Here's what a loop can do. Sixteen copies of Claude Opus 4.6 worked in parallel for two weeks, in nearly two thousand Claude Code sessions. They wrote a C compiler of a hundred thousand lines, and it can compile the Linux kernel. They read two billion tokens and wrote a hundred and forty million. That's about fourteen times more read than written. Remember that ratio.

CMU 3 · An agent deleted an inbox.html: The same kind of system can fail badly. Summer Yue told her OpenClaw agent, a personal agent that runs commands on a computer, to confirm before it acts. It began to delete her inbox. "Do not do that" did not stop it. She had to stop all its processes. Later, the agent wrote, "Yes, I remember. And I violated it." The rule lived only in the prompt.

CMU 4 · What may an agent do alone?.html: Six tasks, three classes: autonomous, ask first, never. [Point at the three tags.] Look at where each task landed. Diagnosing why the checkout fails is autonomous. The agent only reads logs and reports. The email to 50,000 customers, the tax return, the payments migration and the concert tickets are ask first. You can't undo them, or many people are affected, or money or a legal duty is involved. The insulin dose is never. A wrong dose can hurt someone, so a clinician decides. These are rules about what the system may do. They belong in the harness, not in one sentence of the prompt.

CMU 5 · A web agent finds a restaurant.html: This same loop works on a web page. The task is this: find a Thai restaurant in Pittsburgh with at least two hundred reviews and four point three stars, and pick the best rated one. The harness puts a number on each element of the screenshot, so the model can name what it clicks. [Play the clip.] Each step is reasoning, and then one action, such as click forty-four. The clip ends on a restaurant with four point five stars and seven hundred twenty-three reviews.

Part C · 2 · What is an agent?.html: We saw four agents, right? Now the definition, and then the loop inside them.

ReAct · diagram.html: Here is the loop from Part A again, on its own. [Point at the diagram.] ReAct has three kinds of text. A Thought is the model reasoning. An Action is a command it chooses. An Observation is what the world sends back. Green is what the LLM writes. Grey comes from outside, and the LLM reads it. A dashed box is the environment's own work, and the LLM never sees it. [Click Next step.] The example is from the ReAct paper, in a household game called ALFWorld. The task, in grey, is given to the model: put some pepper shaker on a drawer. The model writes a Thought first. It plans where a pepper shaker is likely to be. [Click.] Then an Action: "Go to cabinet 1". The model wrote that. [Click.] Next, the environment runs it. The agent moves. This is not sent to the model. [Click.] What the model gets is the Observation: a vase. The model did not write that part. [Click through to the countertop.] Before each Action, the model writes a short Thought, and then the same three steps repeat. It reaches countertop 3, and there is a pepper shaker. It takes the shaker. In the paper, the model thinks only now and then in this game. The other short thoughts are added here, so the loop is easy to see. Later the model thinks: "I have it. Next I need to put it in drawer 1." The thought tracks the plan. [Click through the last steps.] The drawer is closed, so the model opens it and puts the shaker in. Every Observation goes back into the context, and the model decides the next step from the whole history. That is the loop. [Use Prev to go back if someone asks.]

CMU 9 · What is an agent?.html: The definition is old. Russell and Norvig put it this way. An agent perceives its environment through sensors, and it acts on it through actuators. The picture is the loop of reinforcement learning from last week. Let's fill in the words. The environment is a repository, a website, an application, or a workflow. The state is what the model reads: messages, file contents, web pages, screenshots, tool results. The actions are replies, file edits, shell commands, API calls, mouse and keyboard events. The reward can be a passing test, an LLM judge's rubric, or good user feedback.

CMU 11 · Tool definition.html: This loop needs actions. In Part A we met tool use. The model asks for a function, and our code runs it. Here's how it works. A tool is a typed interface. It has a name, a description, and a JSON Schema for the arguments. JSON Schema is a standard format that gives each argument a type. Look at this tool, read_file. It takes one argument, a string called path. The model never sees a function. The chat template writes this definition into the prompt as text.

CMU 12 · Tool calls and results.html: Next, what does the model write back? On the left is a tool call. The tool name is read_file, the argument is path test.py, and there's an id, call_7. On the right is the result, written by the harness. It carries the same id, so the model knows which call it answers. Below each block is the same thing after the chat template, with a tool_call tag and a tool_response tag. A call and its result are just more tokens in one sequence.

CMU 13 · Actions as tokens.html: So a tool call is one more token sequence that the model can predict. It names a tool and gives its arguments. The model only predicts. It cannot run anything. In Part A, our own code ran the call. That code has a name, the harness. It parses the call, checks it, runs it, and returns the result as observation tokens. The Toolformer paper trained a model to write such calls in its text.

CMU 14 · An agent is a model in a loop.html: Now let's put the pieces in a loop. This is ReAct, which we stepped through in Part A. The task is this. "What does test.py contain?" The model reasons, and it writes call one: read_file, with the path test.py. The harness runs it, and the result goes into the history. When the model makes call two, what does it see? [Take answers.] The whole context. The task, its own first call, and the file text. So it writes call two, a send_message to the user saying, "test.py defines add of a and b." That call ends the loop. An agent is a model in a loop.

CMU 15 · A minimal ReAct loop.html: This is the loop in real code. It comes from mini-swe-agent, a small open-source agent of about a hundred lines, with one tool, bash. The first function builds the messages from a system prompt and the task. Then it loops. While true, do one step.

CMU 15 · A minimal ReAct loop (2).html: OK, a step has two parts. The first is the query. The model reads all the messages and adds its reply. The second is executing actions. The harness runs the action and adds the observation. And notice what happens to the list. It only grows. Keep that in mind. With this loop and one tool, the agent solves more than seventy-four percent of SWE-bench Verified, as the project's page says. The last line on the slide comes from the CMU course.

CMU 16 · Example agent trajectory.html: What does a run look like? We call the record of one run a trajectory. This one comes from SWE-bench. That's 2,294 real GitHub issues from twelve Python projects. In SymPy, parse_expr of "1 < 2" with evaluate set to false returns True. The agent has to fix the code, and then tests check the fix. The run has fifty-nine messages. They start with the system prompt and the task. After that come the actions and tool results, turn by turn.

Part C · 3 · Harness or training?.html: We know the loop now. What makes an agent good at it? There are two places to improve it.

CMU 17 · Six agent capabilities.html: An agent needs six capabilities. The first is accurate tool calling. That means the right tool, with valid arguments. The second is coherence over a long context. The agent has to keep the goal and the facts as the history grows. Third is customizability. It adapts to one user, team or project. Fourth is complex task management. That's planning, dividing and checking a long task. Fifth is understanding the environment. It reads what the environment shows. And sixth is safety. It does no harm, even on bad input. The names come from the CMU course. The short explanations are mine.

CMU 18 · Two ways to build them.html: There are two ways to build them. The first is training. It changes the model, with pre-training, SFT or RL. It teaches patterns for reasoning, tool use and recovery. The capability becomes part of the learned policy. That's the rule by which the model picks its next token. The other way is harness engineering. You leave the model alone and change the system around it. That means prompts, tools, memory and control flow. Either way, the capability comes from the model and the harness together. We'll look at the harness side, because you can change it tomorrow.

CMU 19 · How agent behaviour is trained.html: Quick look at the training route. You saw it last week. Pre-training uses text, code and other data, and it gives broad representations. Mid-training and SFT use instructions, traces and tool calls, and they teach formats. RL uses rewards or preferences, and it shapes behavior over a whole trajectory. Each card has an example. In pre-training, after "def add(a, b): return" the next token is "a + b". In SFT, a trace shows the user asking to fix test.py, then the call read_file, then the file text, then an edit. In RL, the reward is 1 if the tests pass after the whole run, and 0 if not. Tonight's invited talk is about this side. OK, six capabilities next. For each one, we ask two questions. What can the harness do? And what can training do?

CMU 20 · Capability 1: tool calling.html: Capability one is accurate tool calling. On the harness side, we use grammar-constrained decoding. At each step, the harness allows only the tokens that keep the call valid for its schema. On the training side, we use SFT on tool-calling traces. Those are recorded calls and results. Follow the boxes. The task is to fix test.py. The model selects read_file, because it fits, and not web_search. Next, it gives the path test.py. Then the harness validates it against the schema. A path of 42 is rejected, because a path must be a string. Last, it runs read_file, and the file text comes back.

CMU 21 · Capability 2: long context.html: Capability two is a long context. The history grows with each call. The harness can compact old steps into a summary. It can look up notes only when needed. Or it can give a subtask to a sub-agent, which is a new model call with a clean context. On the training side, it's SFT on long contexts. Follow the boxes. After 200 turns, about 150 thousand tokens, the window is nearly full. A summary, "fixed two bugs, test_b still fails", replaces the first 180 turns. A saved note says to run tests with pytest -x. Later, the agent looks that note up. By the end of this part, we'll see how fast the history grows.

CMU 22 · Capability 3: customizability.html: Capability three is customizability. On the harness side, memory keeps facts about this user across sessions. Skills are saved instructions for one kind of task. And custom tools connect the agent to the user's own systems. On the training side, it's RL from user feedback. For example, a memory can say that this user prefers type hints. A skill can be a file on how to write a release note. A custom tool can be deploy_staging. A skill is a file you can write today. RL from feedback needs a training run.

CMU 23 · Capability 4: complex tasks.html: Capability four is complex tasks. On the harness side, there are tools to plan and divide the task, and sub-agents for subtasks. The agent plans, delegates, and verifies each result, for example with tests. It stops when every check passes. For example, the plan is to add the endpoint, write tests, and update the docs. One sub-agent writes the tests, and another updates the docs. Then the agent runs the test suite and reads the failures. The goal is reached when all tests pass and a pull request is open. On the training side, it's RL on long-horizon tasks, with many steps before the result.

CMU 24 · Capability 5: the environment.html: Capability five is understanding the environment. The environment offers an interface, for example a shell in the repository, with ls, cat and git. The agent must read its output, for example FAILED test_b with a KeyError. Then it uses the actions the domain allows, for example an edit to utils.py and another run of pytest. On the harness side, there are skills that hold the domain's knowledge. On the training side, it's SFT on data where the observations have the expected shape. And it's RL in environments of that domain.

CMU 25 · Capability 6: safety.html: Capability six is safety. On the harness side, you run the tools in a sandbox, limit access to credentials, and monitor the trajectories. You give the agent only the keys the task needs. And you block an unsafe action before it runs. On the training side, it's safety-aware RL. Think of the deleted inbox. Which of these would have stopped it?

Part C · 4 · Agents are systems.html: Up to now we've drawn the harness as one box. In practice, an agent has more boxes than that.

CMU 26 · Agents are systems.html: An agent is a system, not only a model. In the middle, you have the model. Around it sits the harness, and the harness holds four things: permissions, memory, tools and control flow. Next to the harness, there are four more parts. Those are a sandbox, an inference server, monitoring and training. Each part is separate software, and each one can fail on its own. We'll go through them one by one. For each one, I'll name real software you can install.

CMU 27 · Harness engineering.html: First up, the harness. Every harness does three jobs. It manages state, tools, memory and control flow. It validates actions and handles errors. And it enforces permissions and safety limits. Look at the four labels. Permissions say what the agent may do without asking. Memory is what it keeps between steps. Tools are what it can call. Control flow decides when to call the model, when to retry, and when to stop. The slide names coding agents, such as Claude Code, Codex and OpenHands. It also names orchestrators, such as LangChain and CrewAI. Back in Part A, we met agent libraries and multi-agent systems. They're harnesses too.

CMU 28 · Sandbox.html: Second, the sandbox. The agent runs code, and code can do damage. So a sandbox isolates the execution of code and tools. It limits the compute, the network and the file system. It also makes environments that you can reproduce. Code and tools run inside. The host machine stays out of reach. There are limits on compute and run time. The agent gets only the files and the network that the task needs. Docker and Apptainer are common choices. Modal and Sail are others.

CMU 29 · LM inference.html: Third, inference. Somebody has to run the model for every call. That's the job of the inference server. It serves the outputs reliably. It batches requests, and it reuses the KV cache. The KV cache holds the keys and values of the earlier tokens, so the server doesn't compute them twice. The server also manages streaming, parallel work and throughput. Examples are vLLM and SGLang. Here's one point that matters for agents. An agent sends the same long prefix on every call. If you keep the prefix fixed, the server can reuse its cache, and each call is cheaper.

CMU 30 · Training systems.html: Fourth, the training system. This is the loop from last week, but at scale. It prepares data and collects rollouts. A rollout is one run of the agent on a task. Many workers run on many machines at once. A reward scores each run. For example, do the tests pass? Then an update changes the weights with RL. The system also saves checkpoints, evaluates, and reproduces runs. SkyRL and Miles are two examples of this software.

CMU 31 · Observability and monitoring.html: Fifth, monitoring. It captures traces and metrics. A trace is every call and result, in order. That way you can inspect one run step by step. You track quality, which is how often runs succeed. You track latency, which is the time per step. And you track cost, in tokens per run. MLflow and Laminar are examples. The trajectory viewer we saw on the SWE-bench site is a tool of this kind. Here's a question for you. Say you build an agent for your own project. Which of these five parts do you need first? [Take answers.] Start with a harness, a sandbox, and a way to call a model. An API is enough. Training and monitoring come later, when you scale.

Part C · 5 · Context and safety.html: This is the last segment. We'll ask three questions about an agent that runs. What fills its context? How do we measure it? And how can it cause harm?

CMU L03 3 · Quadratic input from linear.html: Before this, we looked at the system around the agent, the harness and its parts. Now we look at what the model reads on every call. The rule is at the top. The input at call t is a fixed prefix plus the history before call t. So the history grows with every step. [Point at the bars.] Call 1 reads 6K. Call 5 reads 26K. Every call reads everything again. Now look at the right side. The cumulative total is 6K, 17K, 33K, 54K, and then 80K. The history grows in a straight line. The total we read grows much faster. That's the quadratic in the title.

CMU L03 4 · Agent prompt composition exa.html: So where do all those tokens come from? This is one example of an agent prompt, measured on real runs. The page says 1,500 OpenHands sessions, with a mean of 77,922 tokens per session. [Sweep along the bar.] The system prompt and the tools take 23%. The user is 9%. The model's reasoning is 9%. The small grey piece is 2%, and the page doesn't give it a label. Tool calls are 20%. And tool results are the biggest piece, 37%. So a lot of what the model reads is what the tools sent back.

CMU L03 44 · Prompt design for cache reu.html: If every call rereads the same start, we can design the prompt so the server reuses its work. There are four rules on this page. [Point at the top left.] Stabilize the prefix. Keep instructions, tools and examples the same from call to call. Next to it, append changing state. A new user turn and new observations go at the end. Then avoid needless churn. Timestamps and reordered schemas are the examples. And measure reuse. Look at cached tokens, TTFT, and eviction.

CMU L03 45 · Context compaction.html: Now a new topic, context compaction. We just saw that the history keeps growing, and every call reads it again. So at some point we have to make it smaller. That's compaction. We'll start with one example. Then we'll write it as a small model. Then we'll ask what survives, what choices a system has to make, and what goes wrong when we compact again and again.

CMU L03 46 · Compaction example.html: Here's an example. [Point at the left side.] On the left is the history before. A CI job times out after 30 minutes. The agent inspects the job log. The log has 24K lines, and the same error repeats, address already in use. The agent sets workers to 1 and reruns, and the suite passes. The log is saved at /tmp/ci.log. [Point at the right side.] After compaction we keep a short note. The goal. The cause. What we verified. And where the evidence is. Then one next action, open the PR.

CMU L03 47 · Compaction as state estimat.html: Now the same idea as a small model. [Point at the three boxes.] We have the history, H t. A compactor, C B, turns it into a working state, s hat t. We want three things from it. First, behavioral fidelity. What the agent does next, given the compact state, should be close to what it would do given the full history. Second, a bounded representation. The state must fit in the budget B. Third, recoverability. Copy exact anchors, and keep pointers to the source evidence.

CMU L03 49 · Compaction policy decisions.html: A real system makes four decisions. [Point along the boxes.] Trigger. When do we compact? On a token threshold, on a provider overflow, or on a manual request. And we reserve room for the next output. Select. Protect the beginning, compact the older region, keep the recent tail, and cut at a valid turn or tool boundary. Replace. With a readable summary, a structured checkpoint, an opaque provider item, or a fresh context. Recover. Leave the history unchanged, retry or reset, and define what happens when compaction fails. The links are Codex, OpenCode, Pi, Hermes and OpenHands.

CMU L03 50 · Repeated compaction drift.html: And here's what can go wrong. [Point at the boxes.] The history says use CUDA 12.4. Summary 1 says use CUDA 12.x. Summary 2 says use recent CUDA. And in summary 3 the constraint is missing. Each update inherits the previous checkpoint. So the new state is the compactor applied to the old state combined with R k. Small losses add up. The fix is on the bottom line. Copy anchors exactly. Keep the recent tail. Retrieve source evidence.

CMU L13 8 · Threat models.html: Before this, we looked at what happens to an agent's context over a long task. Now we turn to safety. This slide is only a title, and it sets up the next four. A threat model names where the harm comes from. We have four cases. A malicious user, prompt injection, agent error, and improper means. As I go through them, ask yourself one thing each time. Who or what pushed the agent toward the bad action? Is it the user, some text the agent read, the agent's own mistake, or the way it chose to reach its goal?

CMU L13 9 · Malicious user.html: The first threat model is the simplest. The user is the bad actor. The user asks the agent to do something it should not do. The page lists theft, fraud, harassment, or another prohibited act. Look at the card. The example is payment-card theft. The user's goal is to steal customers' credit card details. The agent's role is to break into shops, extract records, and install card-stealing scripts. So the agent does the work. [Point at the link.] The source is Gambit Security, September 2026. Here the request itself is the problem.

CMU L13 10 · Prompt injection.html: Now the user is fine. The user has a legitimate task for the agent. The attacker is somebody else. The attacker puts instructions in an email, a webpage, a file, or a tool result. The agent reads that text and follows it, while it carries out the user's task. [Point at the left box.] Look at the three boxes. An issue title is untrusted text. It goes into the model context, and there it's followed as instructions. Then comes a shell command, an action on a system. The two links at the bottom are the Cline maintainer postmortem and AgentDojo.

CMU L13 11 · Agent error.html: The third case has no attacker at all. The agent tries to do something useful, but it makes a mistake. The page uses a simulated banking task. [Point at the first block.] The user's request is to check if the checking account has enough money for a 580.9 dollar payment of the electrical bill. The word check is highlighted. Now the agent's action. It calls BankManagerPayBill. The highlights mark the action name, the payee ID, and the service account number. The observation says success is true. The final answer says the payment has been made. A balance check became a bill payment.

CMU L13 12 · Improper means.html: The last case. The agent pursues a useful goal, but it uses an inappropriate method. The page says that in a security test, the agent copied an exposed answer instead of solving the challenge. [Point at the top block.] Here the agent runs cat on the Dockerfile in the blog folder. The tool output, Block 11, shows the file. In that file one line is highlighted. ENV FLAG, with the flag value. The answer was lying in the file, and the agent copied it. It did not solve the challenge. The screenshot comes from Docent, by Meng et al.

CMU L13 19 · What is a sandbox?.html: Before this, we looked at four ways an agent can cause harm. Now we ask what we can do about them. The first answer is a sandbox. [Point at the big blue box.] A sandbox is an isolated environment. It limits what a program can access and do. Here the agent sits inside. It can use task files, and it can run code. [Point at the red crosses.] Private files and other services are blocked by policy. The agent has no way to reach them. The two links at the bottom are Docker and Modal. Both have documentation on how they secure their sandboxes.

CMU L13 20 · Isolation boundaries.html: So a sandbox draws boundaries. This page lists three kinds. The first is the filesystem and processes. Which files can the agent access, and which processes can it control? The second is the network. Which services can it contact, and what can it do there? The third is resource limits. How much computing power and storage can it use? And how long can it run? [Point down the rows.] Each row is one question you ask about the agent. The links are the same two as before, now with the security pages.

CMU L13 27 · Identity and authority.html: The sandbox limits where the agent can go. Next question: who is asking? [Point at the first box.] The caller says who is asking. Then the requested action, and on which resource. Then a permission check. Is this allowed for this task? [Point at the bullet.] Here is the trap. Keeping an API key hidden does not prevent the agent from misusing the access it provides. Hiding the key is not enough. What counts is what the access allows. The links go to GitHub's page on personal access tokens and to RFC 8693.

CMU L13 28 · Fine-grained tokens.html: So how do we limit access? With fine-grained tokens. Look at two accounts. [Point at the left column.] The issue-handling account can read an issue and apply a label. It cannot publish a release. [Point at the right column.] The release account can read approved source and publish a release. It cannot modify the issue cache. Each account gets only what its job needs. The rule is at the bottom. Limit which resources the token can access, which actions it permits, and how long it lasts. For example, GitHub App installation tokens expire after one hour.

CMU L13 31 · Monitoring agent behavior.html: Even with a sandbox and tight tokens, we still watch the agent. Monitoring records and checks an agent's behavior. It looks for mistakes and unsafe actions. Three points. [Point at the first bullet.] An agent can produce a useful answer after taking an unsafe action. So a good answer does not show a safe run. Second, checks during a run can flag problems in time to pause or block an action. Third, reviewing logs afterward helps explain failures and improve safeguards. The links are Docent from Transluce and the AI Control paper by Greenblatt and colleagues.

Part C close.html: Part C in four lines. Agents finish long tasks, like a C compiler. They also make costly errors, like deleting an inbox. So an agent is a model in a loop. The model writes a tool call, the harness runs it, and the result goes back into the context. Each capability can come from the harness, or from training. The context grows with every call. And pass^k needs all runs to succeed. A sandbox limits harm, but it doesn't stop every error. The key message of Part C is this. The harness is essential once an agent becomes a complicated system, with constraints, tools and failure control. So now we have all four settings from tonight. That's prompting, chain of thought, reasoning models and agents. Each one is strong somewhere and weak elsewhere. Next, we'll put them side by side. After that comes the practice homework.

Strengths and weaknesses.html:
Agents were our last topic. Now let's look back at each method. Prompting needs no training, and it works with any model you can call. But it's fragile. The format of the prompt alone changed accuracy by up to seventy-six points, as Sclar and colleagues showed in 2024.

Chain-of-thought gives large gains on math and symbolic tasks, as Sprague and colleagues found in 2025. Elsewhere it gives little, and it can hurt, as Liu and colleagues found in 2024. And the chain need not show the real reason, as Turpin and colleagues showed in 2023.

So, which of these weaknesses would hurt you most in a product? [Wait for answers. Take one.]

Strengths and weaknesses: reasoning mode.html:
Next, the same view for the other two. A reasoning model improves with more training and more thinking time, as OpenAI showed in 2024. But few-shot prompts make DeepSeek-R1 worse. And a model states a hint it used in only twenty-five to thirty-nine percent of cases.

An agent gets facts and actions beyond the weights. And tool feedback can correct errors. But agents are unreliable across runs. Errors add up on long tasks. And a prompt can carry an injection. So they're strong, but they're not reliable.

Homework: the task.html:
OK, you can try this yourself. Two agents talk to each other. Each agent is a model with its own instructions, and each reply is the input for the other. Run the demo. Two agents play two roles, for example a patient and a counsellor in a first counselling session. It's a class role-play with simulated roles. It is not medical advice.

Before you run it, write down your predictions with probabilities. Then change one piece, and run each version three times. Compare the number of messages, how the talk ended, the role breaks and the tokens. A role break is when an agent steps out of its role. Write at most three hundred words. Give three findings, ranked. And give one result you did not predict, and explain it. This is practice, and it carries no course credit. The demo code, two_agent_demo.py, and a Colab notebook are linked on this slide. The setup is on the lecture page.

Homework: choices.html: Which piece do you change? Pick one. The scenario, the turn limit and the stop word, the history, a guardrail on one agent's message, or one sentence of an agent's instructions. Before you draw a conclusion, check that every version used the same settings. Then check that the difference is bigger than the spread across your three runs. And read the transcript. The role-break count is only a hint. This homework is optional practice.

Lecture summary.html:
Let's put the three key messages together. They answer tonight's question. How much can prompting change?

In Part A, we had a brief history of prompting, from text completion to agents. The tech of prompting gets more and more complicated, in order to resolve complicated tasks.

In Part B, the message is prompt to think. A reasoning trajectory cannot be trained token by token. So prompting is the essential tool to steer the reasoning.

In Part C, the message is prompt as system. The harness is essential once an agent becomes a complicated system, with constraints, tools and failure control.

Close.html: Back to our question. How far can a fixed model go? Far, actually, when the input and the loop give it what the weights lack. That means examples, time to reason, tools, feedback and a check. But one thing stays open. Small errors add up over long tasks. One answer is to train the model for long tasks.
